# How to Read the Evidence in This Book {.unnumbered}

::: {.content-visible unless-format="epub"}
[]{#how-to-read-the-evidence-in-this-book}
:::

Imagine deciding whether to spend a limited training budget on a programme advertised to “raise productivity by 20%.” The promise sounds large enough to justify the purchase. But if the reported improvement reflects who enrolled or measures a short test rather than work performance, buying the programme may not deliver the benefit you need. The spending decision turns on what the number actually compares.

Did participants improve relative to their own earlier performance, or relative to people who did not receive the training? The answer changes what we can infer about the programme. We also need to know how people entered those groups and whether the outcome measures the benefit the organization wants.

The following questions help turn a memorable result into a claim we can evaluate.

[]{#begin-with-the-claim}

Begin by asking what the training claim promises. Reporting that participants improved is **descriptive**; using their earlier results to forecast later performance is **predictive**. Saying that the programme produced the improvement is **causal**, while explaining how it did so is **mechanistic**. Extending the conclusion to other people or workplaces adds a claim of **generality**. These claims require different kinds of evidence.

The training participants might improve because of the programme, because unusually motivated people enrolled, or because a temporary slump ended. An association between attendance and improvement would not separate those explanations. Even a credible causal effect would leave questions about why the programme worked and whether it would work elsewhere.

## Examine the comparison, measure, and estimate {#read-each-boundary-in-four-moves}

A useful account of evidence identifies the comparison, the outcome, and the explanation being tested. Methodological details in the footnotes let you examine a result more closely.

For the training example, knowing that the outcome was a short knowledge test directs attention to what participants learned. A follow-up measure of workplace performance would answer a different practical question.

[]{#separate-size-from-certainty}

Ask how large the estimated difference is in meaningful units, how uncertain the estimate is, and whether the range of plausible effects would matter for the decision. Read the result alongside its comparison, including the denominator and study condition when a proportion is reported. A percentage of participants who acted once is different from a percentage of all opportunities to act. In a hypothetical service team, an increase from 10 to 12 completed cases per hour and an increase from 100 to 120 are both 20%, but they add 2 and 20 cases per hour respectively. The starting level and units make the gain interpretable.

A *p*-value is not an effect size or the probability that a theory is true. A statistically significant result can be too small to matter in practice, while an imprecisely estimated effect may still include important possibilities. Magnitude, uncertainty, and practical relevance need separate attention.

[]{#ask-what-was-measured}

Trust, happiness, attention, and similar constructs are inferred from observations such as answers, choices, response times, or physiological measures. Each measure captures some aspects more directly than others.

For example, a person who rejects an unequal offer might dislike inequality, want to punish the proposer, or be concerned about reputation. The rejection alone does not identify the motive. A convincing explanation needs a comparison that helps distinguish the alternatives, rather than a new label for the same observation.

## Assess the evidence across studies and settings {#distinguish-an-illustration-from-evidence}

Fictional cases and classroom demonstrations help make an idea concrete. They show how something could happen. A study investigates a specified comparison; replications examine whether the result survives new samples or implementations. Field studies examine behavior in everyday or organizational settings and may be observational or experimental. Formal models make assumptions and their implications explicit.

A meta-analysis combines studies but inherits difficulties in the available literature, including selective publication and differences in measurement. No source type answers every question. Look for the evidence that bears on the particular claim.

[]{#treat-replication-as-information-not-a-verdict}

A failed replication may weaken confidence in an original finding, reveal a boundary, or expose a difference in measurement or implementation. Comparing the studies helps distinguish these possibilities. A successful replication strengthens support across the conditions tested.

Low precision, flexible analysis, and selective publication can make a literature look more convincing than it is. Preregistration, transparent reporting, accessible data and code, and independent replication help readers examine these problems. [Appendix E's evidence-status map](appendices/appendix-f-when-evidence-breaks.qmd#famous-findings-after-replication) applies this approach to prominent behavioral findings.

[]{#ask-whether-the-finding-travels}

Return to the training claim. Results from volunteers may differ from results among employees required to attend; a short course may work differently when instructors, incentives, or opportunities to practise change. The outcome and follow-up period matter too.

An actual comparison shows how much this can matter. DellaVigna and Linos (2022) compared published experiments on nudges with trials run by two US government nudge units. The average increase in the targeted behavior was **8.7 percentage points** in the journal sample and **1.4 points** in the nudge-unit sample. Both sets contained randomized trials, yet reading only the published studies would have suggested a much larger typical effect. Randomization within trials does not randomize which interventions are studied or which results reach journals. [Chapter 40](chapters/40-choice-architecture-the-environment-gets-a-vote.qmd#choice-architecture-the-environment-gets-a-vote) examines the roles of publication selection and differences in interventions; neither average is a promise about your next project.

Generalization becomes more informative when we specify which differences should matter and test them. “It depends” is the beginning of an explanation only when we can say what it depends on.

## A six-question evidence audit

For any claim you might use, ask:

1. **What exactly is being claimed?** Description, prediction, causation, mechanism, or generality?
2. **What is the comparison?** Compared with what, for whom, and over what period?
3. **How large and uncertain is the estimate?** Consider the units and the range of plausible values.
4. **What else could explain the observation?** Identify a competing account.
5. **Where might the finding change?** Consider the population, task, and setting.
6. **What evidence would change my confidence?** Make the belief open to revision.

You do not need to become a methods specialist before reading the book. Keep these questions nearby, and return to them when a result surprises you or seems useful. [Appendix C](appendices/appendix-literature-review.qmd#conducting-and-writing-a-literature-review) shows how to use them across a literature, explain what is known, and identify what remains unresolved. [Appendix D](appendices/appendix-e-how-behavioral-evidence-is-built.qmd#running-an-experimental-study-from-question-to-credible-evidence) turns a research question into a study; [Appendix E](appendices/appendix-f-when-evidence-breaks.qmd#when-evidence-breaks-the-replication-crisis-and-research-integrity) explains how replication and research integrity shape the evidence available to us.
